claims.text: FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles have inherent compositional heterogeneity in their initially solid state.
Localized surface atomic segregation forms compositional hotspots in FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles.
The compositional hotspots have a lower local melting point than the surrounding nanoparticle material.
The lower-melting compositional hotspots trigger the onset of the phase transition.
Localized surface segregation governs the progression of the phase transition after its onset.
Surface segregation produces regions enriched in lower-melting-point elements.
Regions enriched in lower-melting-point elements act as nucleation sites for premelting.
Premelting initiated at segregated surface regions accelerates the overall phase transition.
A surface passivation layer can inhibit atomic segregation in FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles.
Suppressing surface segregation with passivation delays the appearance of local premelting features.
Under identical heating conditions, untreated nanoparticles will exhibit local premelting at a lower temperature than passivated nanoparticles.
Passivated nanoparticles will maintain a more uniform surface composition than untreated nanoparticles during heating.
Pristine FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles exhibit early surface segregation and corresponding local premelting at relatively low temperatures.
Unintentional oxidation can obscure the proposed relationship between surface segregation and premelting.
Variation in heating ramp rate can obscure the proposed relationship between surface segregation and premelting.

Identical premelting onset temperatures and similar transition progression in the two groups, despite demonstrably different surface compositions, would falsify the proposed causal role of surface segregation.
